meta.title: Who really said "I am under no obligation to make sense to you"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Carroll and not the Mad Hatter: "obligation" is not in either Alice book. The nearest real sentence belongs to an astrophysicist.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I am under no obligation to make sense to you'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to the Mad Hatter or the Cheshire Cat. The word "obligation" appears nowhere in either Alice book.

answer.label: Not Lewis Carroll — and not the Hatter
answer.authorDates: Author unestablished · circulated as a Mad Hatter line
answer.sourceLine: Carroll did not write this. The word “obligation” does not occur once in either Alice book, and across twelve of his English works it appears exactly twice — in A Tangled Tale and Sylvie and Bruno, both in ordinary senses about debts and about a reader being released from believing a story. Neither is this sentence or anything near it. The nearest genuinely documented line with this shape is Neil deGrasse Tyson’s ↗ — “The universe is under no obligation to make sense to you” — but that is about the universe, not about a person, and we are not claiming one produced the other. Who wrote the version on the mugs, we could not establish.

source.excerpt: “I am under no obligation to make sense to you.”
trail: We downloaded the Project Gutenberg texts of twelve of Carroll’s English works — Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, Through the Looking-Glass, Alice’s Adventures Under Ground, The Nursery “Alice”, The Hunting of the Snark, Phantasmagoria and Other Poems, Songs from Alice, Sylvie and Bruno, Sylvie and Bruno Concluded, A Tangled Tale, The Game of Logic and Symbolic Logic — flattened every line break so no phrase could hide across a line ending, and searched 2.1 million characters of it. The sentence does not occur. “Under no obligation” does not occur. “Make sense to you” does not occur.

We read the only two places the word appears at all. In A Tangled Tale a speaker “ought to discharge one obligation before contracting any fresh liabilities”; in Sylvie and Bruno the narrator releases his reader “from any obligation he may feel to believe this part of my story”. Carroll uses the word twice across the twelve books we searched, in the register of a mathematician being polite. His diaries, letters and pamphlets are not in that corpus, so this is a count of the published books, not of everything he ever wrote.

We also ran the phrase through a full-text search of the whole of Wikiquote — an insource: query, which reads the raw wikitext of every page on the site — rather than only Carroll’s own page. The wording “under no obligation to make sense to you” appears on exactly one page in all of Wikiquote: Neil deGrasse Tyson’s ↗, where the sourced line reads “The universe is under no obligation to make sense to you”, given as an epigram at page 13 of Astrophysics for People in a Hurry (W. W. Norton, 2017). It is a different sentence with a different subject, and we record it as a neighbour, not a source.

Neither the Wonderland page ↗ nor Carroll’s own page ↗ lists the line, in their sourced sections or their misattributed ones. As with any absence, that tells you nobody has filed it — not that it is genuine.
source.excerptNote: The Hatter it is usually given to is a poor fit even before you check the text. Carroll’s Hatter is not defiant about making sense; he is confident he is making sense, and is baffled that Alice cannot keep up. Defiance is a modern reading of the character, not the one on the page.

source.rightsNote: No rights badge. Carroll’s writing is in the public domain, but this sentence is not his, and its actual origin is unknown to us — so there is no work whose rights we can report. A sentence of unknown modern authorship is not safe to treat as free to reuse simply because it is attached to a Victorian name.

author.name: Lewis Carroll
author.heading: About the name on the graphic
author.bio: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson — Lewis Carroll on the title page — taught mathematics at Christ Church, Oxford for most of his adult life, and wrote the two Alice books and a shelf of logic puzzles alongside it. His actual sentences are odd in a specific way: precise, deadpan, and usually about the rules of language rather than about feelings. That is worth knowing, because the lines invented for him are almost always the opposite — warm, motivational, and about you.

cite.sourceCitation: No located source. The sentence appears in none of Lewis Carroll's published works, which use the word "obligation" twice in unrelated senses. Compare, documented: Neil deGrasse Tyson, Astrophysics for People in a Hurry (New York: W. W. Norton, 2017), 13 - "The universe is under no obligation to make sense to you."

items.who: Lewis Carroll, in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
items.why: “Obligation” appears zero times in Wonderland ↗ and zero times in Through the Looking-Glass ↗. The sentence is in neither, in any form.

items.who: The Mad Hatter (or the Cheshire Cat)
items.why: Both are given the line on prints and tattoos; neither says it. The Hatter’s actual dialogue in the tea-party chapter of Wonderland ↗ is about watches, butter and a quarrel with Time.

Wikiquote sources ↗ “The universe is under no obligation to make sense to you” to Astrophysics for People in a Hurry (2017), p. 13. Different subject, different claim, and we have no evidence connecting the two — but if you want a real quotation in this shape, it is his and not Carroll’s.

misattribution.truthLine: Checkable in seconds: the full text of Wonderland ↗ contains no “obligation” at all. Who wrote the sentence remains open, and we would rather leave it open than guess.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is a boundary-setting line dressed as whimsy, which is exactly what a Mad Hatter quote is expected to do in 2026 — it reads as permission to be unintelligible on purpose. Carroll’s Wonderland gets recruited for that job constantly, because everybody remembers it as the book about nonsense.

What the book is actually about is stricter than that. Carroll was a logician, and the joke in Wonderland is almost always that the creatures are reasoning correctly from absurd premises — the Hatter’s riddle, the Cat’s proof that it is mad, the trial’s rules invented mid-sentence. Nobody in it claims a right not to make sense. They all insist they already do.
